title: Primary keys
description: Every table has a primary key: a column (or set of columns) that uniquely identifies each row and can never repeat or be NULL. Write a query that returns the `id` and `name` of every department, ordered by `id`.
hints: 💡 SQL concept to consider: PRIMARY KEY

A primary key is a promise the database enforces for you: no two rows in the table can ever share the same value in that column, and it can never be NULL - so it's always safe to use to point at one specific row from anywhere else in the schema.
Select id and name from departments, and order the result by id.
expected_behavior: Returns id and name for every department, ordered by id.
solution: SELECT id, name FROM departments ORDER BY id;
explanation: departments.id is declared SERIAL PRIMARY KEY: Postgres auto-generates a unique integer for it and rejects any INSERT or UPDATE that would duplicate an existing value - that guarantee is what makes it safe for other tables (like employees.department_id) to reference it.
postgres_note: SERIAL is Postgres shorthand for "INTEGER + an auto-incrementing sequence" - the newer, standard-SQL way to spell the same thing is GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY.
